The original light was Argand style lamps mounted in front of parabolic reflectors. In 1839, Cape Hatteras was fitted with eighteen 14” reflectors. By 1849, the light had been upgraded to fifteen 21” reflectors. This system used whale oil for fuel and, if in perfect operating condition, produced a medium intensity light that could be seen up to 20 miles.

The original 112-ft., 18-lamp lighthouse at Cape Hatteras was designed to warn mariners of the “Graveyard” for up to 18 miles out to sea. However, the beacon was frequently too dim to be seen before ships helplessly foundered upon the treacherous shallows. As a result, hundreds of ships sank off the Hatteras coast, including the U.S.S. In July 1797, Congress set aside $44,000. for the building of a lighthouse on Cape Hatteras Island as well as a lighted beacon to facilitate safe travel for ships near the Harbor of Ocracoke in North Carolina. The construction was started and completed in 1803. The original lighting system of the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse consisted of 18 lamps with 14-inch reflectors. The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse stood a miniscule 112 feet above sea level. According to USN LT. David D. Porter, the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse as it was originally constructed was virtually ineffective. The steamer ships that ran that same shipping line at night had brighter lights than the lighthouse and were often mistaken by the ships captains as the lighthouse beacon therefore drawing the larger ships closer to shore and into the breakers that eventually would run them aground.

By 1848, the 18 lamps in the original housing were replaced by 15 lamps with 21-inch reflectors that allowed the 18 mile visible distance to be increased to a 20 mile visible distance. In 1854, the first-order light was created and installed in the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse. The Fresnel Lens included a flashing white light that replaced the original lamps and reflectors.
